papers.title: Causal event structure shapes convergent reactivation signatures in human cortex and language model
papers.abstract: Humans adapt to changing environments by understanding the latent causal structure of events, and modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly exhibit analogous abilities. However, elucidating how causal knowledge is represented and integrated in the human brain and in LLMs poses a substantial challenge for cognitive science. To address this, we combine topological analysis of representational manifolds with neuroscientific analyses of reactivation. We find that event-level causal relations modulate temporally structured neural reactivation in the human brain, particularly in the angular gyrus, precuneus and prefrontal cortex. By contrast, LLMs express these relations through positionally structured representational reactivation. Despite these differences, the resulting reactivation patterns exhibit similar intrinsic manifold structure across the two systems. Together, these findings suggest that the human brain and LLM share a common principle for organizing causal knowledge.

papers.title: Glymphatic Imaging in Multiple Sclerosis: Microstructural Constraints on DTI-ALPS and Clinical Relevance of gBOLD-CSF Coupling in Relation to Sleep and Disability
papers.abstract: The glymphatic system is the waste clearance pathway in the central nervous system. Although its dysfunction has been associated with several neurological disorders, its role in multiple sclerosis (MS) remains poorly understood. This system is thought to be particularly active during sleep, yet the relationship between sleep metrics and MRI-derived markers of glymphatic activity has been scarcely explored. In this study, we aimed to perform a multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment of glymphatic function in MS and investigate its association with sleep parameters, clinical disability, disease duration and MRI-derived structural markers. The study included 22 patients (34.3{+/-}10.1 years; 16 female) with relapsing-remitting MS and 26 healthy controls (32.2{+/-}5.7 years; 18 female), all of whom underwent 3.0 Tesla MRI. Glymphatic function was assessed using diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index and global blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coupling. In addition, sleep micro- and macrostructural features, clinical disability, disease duration, along with mean diffusivity (MD), lateral ventricular, choroid plexus volumes and lesion load were evaluated. Patients showed reduced DTI-ALPS index, though this difference became only a trend after controlling for MD. No significant group differences were observed in global BOLD signal-CSF coupling. However, in patients, the weaker coupling was associated with longer total sleep time, lower arousal index, greater disability and lateral ventricle enlargement, whereas the DTI-ALPS index showed no significant correlations with any of the measures. Together, these findings challenge the assumption that DTI-ALPS can serve as a reliable marker of glymphatic function in demyelinating diseases such as MS, where disease-related alterations in white matter microstructure can confound diffusion-based measures. In contrast, gBOLD-CSF coupling showed associations with sleep, clinical disability and structural changes in patients, despite the absence of a significant group-level difference. This finding suggests that gBOLD-CSF coupling may capture individual variability in glymphatic-related dynamics relevant to sleep and the clinical expression of MS.

papers.title: Cell-type-specific encoding of effort-based decision-making in the dorsal raphe nucleus
papers.abstract: Effort-based decision-making, the process of weighing reward benefits against effort costs, is essential for adaptive behavior. Although the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) contributes to reward processing and effort-related behaviors, how specific DRN neuronal subtypes contribute to effort-based decision-making remains poorly understood. Using fiber photometry to record DRN serotonergic and GABAergic neurons during an effort-based decision-making task, we found that tonic fluctuations in DRN serotonergic activity were selectively associated with persistent selection of the high-value option. Furthermore, we found that while neither neuronal population was sensitive to relative reward magnitude, effort expenditure selectively enhanced decision- and reward-related signals carried by serotonergic and GABAergic neurons, respectively. Together, these findings support a cell type-specific model in which serotonergic activity provides a signal linking persistent motivational states to effortful choice, whereas GABAergic activity may contribute to evaluating or updating reward outcomes after effort expenditure. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENTChoosing whether a reward is worth the effort required to obtain it is essential for adaptive behavior, yet the neural mechanisms underlying this process remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify distinct contributions of serotonin- and GABAergic neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus, a major source of brain serotonin, to effort-based decision-making. Serotonergic neurons were preferentially engaged in sustained motivational state and action selection, and GABAergic neurons in the processing of reward outcomes following costly actions. Our findings reveal a cell type-specific organization of effort-based reward seeking in the dorsal raphe nucleus and provide a framework for understanding how motivational states, decisions, and reward outcomes are coordinated.

papers.title: Pial arteries bend with every heartbeat
papers.abstract: Arterial pulsations are thought to drive perivascular transport by displacing vessel walls radially. In 11 awake mice, all pial arteries also bend with each heartbeat, displacing the wall by three times the pulse-related dilatation per wall, while veins barely move. The bend has a spatial period of about 20 diameters, arrives with the dilatation, at above 1.6 m/s, and dissipates 450 times less energy in the wall.

papers.title: Dysregulation of cAMP-PKA-mediated mechanisms disrupts basal synaptic function in the absence of presynaptic FMRP
papers.abstract: The regulation of presynaptic mechanisms by the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) remains incompletely understood despite their potential importance to synaptic dysfunction reported in Fragile X syndrome. We combined post-developmental, cell-specific deletion of FMRP in dentate granule cells of the hippocampus with optogenetics, whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology and super resolution imaging. The selective loss of FMRP in DG cells did not alter their intrinsic excitability. The amplitude of synaptic currents was reduced at the output mossy fiber synapses in the absence of presynaptic FMRP, whereas short-term facilitation remained intact. We demonstrate that basal synaptic activity is regulated by PKA at mature mossy fiber synapses, and our results indicate alterations in cAMP-PKA signaling and a potential reduction in the readily releasable pool size in mossy fiber boutons lacking FMRP. Presynaptic FMRP is therefore required for efficient basal neurotransmission at mature mossy fiber synapses and likely acts through cAMP-PKA-dependent signaling pathway. Significance statementThe fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) has been extensively studied as a regulator of postsynaptic mechanisms. However, its physiological functions in presynaptic terminals remain incompletely understood. Using post-developmental, cell-specific deletion of FMRP, we show that presynaptic FMRP is required to maintain efficient basal neurotransmission at hippocampal mossy fiber synapses and identify cAMP-PKA signaling as a potential mechanism for this effect. Taken together, these results highlight a physiological role for presynaptic FMRP during basal synaptic activity and demonstrate how time-controlled gene-editing approaches via viral infection can distinguish primary molecular functions from developmental compensations, thereby shedding new light on both the presynaptic function of FMRP and the pathophysiology of Fragile X syndrome. HighlightsO_LIPresynaptic loss of FMRP reduces basal synaptic activity at hippocampal Mf synapses. C_LIO_LIBasal synaptic activity is regulated by PKA in adult Mf synapses. C_LIO_LIAC-cAMP-PKA pathway is impaired during basal synaptic activity in the absence of presynaptic FMRP. C_LIO_LIRRP size is very likely reduced in AZs at Mf terminals. C_LI

papers.title: Multisensory perceptual decision-making persists as alertness fades, even in the absence of an overt response
papers.abstract: Momentary declines in alertness are common in everyday life, yet we must continue to make rapid and accurate decisions from multiple sensory signals that may converge or conflict. Here we investigated multisensory perceptual decision-making across the wake-sleep transition. Participants performed an audio-tactile spatial localisation task while electroencephalography tracked spontaneous fluctuations in alertness. Although drowsiness slowed responses and increased omissions, participants remained largely accurate, and the behavioural influence of congruent and conflicting tactile information persisted. Behavioural modelling revealed slower evidence accumulation and increased decision boundaries. Stimulus- and response-related neural patterns remained robustly decodable across alertness states, despite changes in their temporal dynamics but multisensory congruency was no longer reliably decoded during drowsiness. Brain signatures of lateralized motor preparation persisted during behavioural omissions and, under multisensory conflict, might even favour the competing response. Declining alertness does not uniformly degrade multisensory perceptual decision-making but selectively alters the processes linking sensory information to action.

papers.title: Vertical climbing in mice: a translationally relevant measure of pain-related impact on natural behaviour
papers.abstract: Despite urgent need for better analgesics, drug development has been complicated by incomplete bench-to-bedside translation. A likely contributing factor is the poor connection between the experimenter-evoked pain-related measures often used in preclinical models, and the clinical symptoms, like broader functional impairment, reported by patients. Here, we asked whether vertical climbing, a species-specific elective behaviour in mice, could serve as a measure of pain-related impairment. We tested male and female mice in a wide range of pain-related models including models of post-operative pain, inflammatory injury, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, cancer-induced bone pain, fibrous dysplasia, neuropathic pain, migraine-related pain and facial neuropathy. Vertical climbing was reduced in all models, across five different laboratories, demonstrating the robustness and consistency of this type of behaviour as a novel pain-related outcome measure. Reduced climbing correlated significantly with established pain-related measures, but its time course diverged from that of evoked mechanical allodynia, while aligned more closely with other non-evoked behaviours, like burrowing, home cage activity, wheel running or weight bearing. Pharmacological validation was bidirectional: gabapentin restored climbing in mice with neuropathic injury, and naltrexone reinstated the climbing deficit in mice that had recovered from intraplantar CFA, consistent with persistent pain held in remission by endogenous opioid signalling. Overall, our results indicate that voluntary vertical climbing is a stable, elective behaviour that provides a robust and translationally relevant measure of pain-related functional impairment in mice.

papers.title: High-throughput serial two-photon tomography with BakingTray and BrainSaw
papers.abstract: Volumetric imaging is increasingly important in fields such as neuroscience, where quantifying structure and mapping features are inherently three-dimensional problems. Block-face serial two-photon tomography (STPT) has emerged as a powerful approach for high-resolution, whole-organ volumetric imaging. STPT avoids complex sample preparation and balances image quality, speed, and scalability. However, STPT remains niche, in part because of the absence of flexible, general-purpose control software. Here we present BakingTray, an open-source software platform for STPT that extends ScanImage. BakingTrays modular framework accommodates diverse hardware configurations and allows users to build systems customised to their needs. Twelve such systems, which we call BrainSaws, have been constructed worldwide since 2016, with more under construction, and have so far contributed to 35 research papers. The three systems at the Sainsbury Wellcome Centre alone have acquired over 7,000 samples in a busy multi-user facility. We demonstrate the platform across its core neuroscience applications: electrode track localisation, brain-wide cell counting, and bulk projection mapping. Beyond these, we map the cell-type-specific synaptic output of inhibitory neurons in the ventral lateral geniculate nucleus and, with whole-mount staining, amyloid plaques brain-wide in a mouse model of Alzheimers disease. BakingTray is a mature platform for groups or facilities needing a customised volumetric imaging solution, whether built new or converted cheaply from an existing two-photon microscope.

papers.title: Season-long head acceleration exposure, prior contact-sport history, and cognitive performance in British amateur American football players
papers.abstract: Background: Head acceleration events (HAEs) are common in contact sports, but season-long exposure and its relationship with cognitive performance in amateur British American football remain poorly characterised. Methods: Thirty male players were recruited from three British American football teams. Cognitive performance was assessed pre-season, mid-season, and post-season using the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool 6 and computerised Stroop, 2-back, Go/No-go, and visual-search tasks. Seasonal cognitive analyses included 23 participants with available data. HAEs were quantified using helmet-mounted accelerometers; exposure-linked analyses were restricted to 19 participants who provided sufficiently complete sensor recordings across contact training sessions and competitive matches. Seasonal cognitive changes were assessed using mixed-effects models. Associations of in-season HAE metrics and previous contact-sport seasons with global cognitive change were examined using simple linear regression and elastic-net regression. Results: In the 19-participant exposure-linked cohort, prior contact-sport exposure showed the strongest nominal univariate association with worse global cognitive change (r squared = 0.337, p = 0.009), although this did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons (Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted p = 0.055). Corrected nested cross-validation indicated little out-of-sample performance for the multivariable elastic-net model (r = 0.144, predictive R squared = -0.008). Although previous contact-sport seasons had the largest standardised coefficient in the final full-cohort fit, predictor retention varied substantially across resamples. Conclusion: Prior contact-sport exposure showed the strongest exploratory association with relatively worse global cognitive change, whereas in-season HAE metrics showed weaker associations. However, the multivariable model did not demonstrate useful out-of-sample predictive performance, and the small exposure-linked cohort precludes firm conclusions regarding the relative importance of individual predictors.

papers.title: The female larval fly CNS connectome: first draft
papers.abstract: We release an enhanced FIB-SEM volume and associated neuron, mitochondria, synapse and glia automated segmentations for the complete, gap- and artifact-free central nervous system of the first instar female larval Drosophila melanogaster. Segmentation data is largely unproofread besides select neurons in the premotor and proprioceptive system and select subvolumes where synapses have been manually annotated, serving as training and evaluation data. The dataset represents the first complete central nervous system of the larval fly, and now awaits substantial improvement of machine vision approaches that effectively leverage domain knowledge for the automated yet data-guided proofreading, or substantial and costly human proofreading. All the data and methods are publicly available for further improvement and analysis.

papers.title: Multiscale structural MRI differences among collegiate American football players, cross-country runners, and non-athletes
papers.abstract: Structural differences observed in collision-sport athletes may reflect repetitive head-impact exposure, broader effects of athletic training, or pre-existing individual variation, making inclusion of a non-collision athlete group important for interpretation of any differences seen. Here, structural T1-weighted MRI data from 17 collegiate American football players, 16 cross-country runners, and 9 non-athletes were analyzed using FSL voxel-based morphometry (VBM), FIRST subcortical volumetry and vertex-wise shape analysis, and FAST whole-brain tissue segmentation. Spatial inference used permutation testing with threshold-free cluster enhancement and family-wise error correction, while scalar analyses used multiplicity-corrected procedures. FAST-derived absolute tissue volumes were also examined in a sensitivity analysis adjusting for FreeSurfer estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV). VBM showed recurrent brainstem-centered differences, with non-athletes showing greater local gray matter measures than both athlete groups, whereas football players showed greater brainstem measures than runners. FIRST vertex-wise analysis identified corrected differences involving the brainstem and selected subcortical structures, while no total FIRST structure volume survived false discovery rate correction. Unadjusted FAST analysis identified a CSF group effect, F(2, 24.38) = 11.46, p < .001, q = .001. After eTIV adjustment, the CSF group effect remained, F(2, 38) = 14.30, q < .001, and a white matter group effect was also identified, F(2, 38) = 9.59, q < .001; gray matter and total segmented tissue did not show corrected adjusted effects. These findings indicate that structural variation depends on anatomical scale, comparison group, and head-size adjustment and cannot be attributed uniquely to collision-sport exposure.

papers.title: Altered Aperiodic EEG Activity in Adolescents with Neurofibromatosis Type 1
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe balance between excitatory and inhibitory neuronal signalling (E/I balance), proposed as a key mechanism controlling neuronal activity, is disrupted in many neurodevelopmental conditions. One such condition is Neurofibromatosis Type 1, a monogenic neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by increased inhibitory tone. While previous research suggests that E/I balance may be altered in infancy, it is unknown whether E/I balance remains altered during adolescence in NF1. Here we investigated this question using the aperiodic exponent of the resting electroencephalogram (EEG) power spectrum, a proposed electrophysiological index of E/I balance. MethodThe aperiodic exponent of the EEG power spectrum ( 1/f) was estimated for 16 adolescents with NF1 diagnosis aged 11-16, and 16 age- and sex-matched neurotypical controls. General linear models (GLM) were fit to estimate effects of NF1 diagnosis, age and their interaction on aperiodic exponent. We also estimated the peak dominant frequency and power in oscillatory activity of the EEG signal and fitted the same structure of GLM models. Cognitive assessments across domains of memory, executive function and attention were also analysed with GLM to examine brain-cognition associations. ResultsThe NF1 group had higher aperiodic exponent compared to neurotypical controls, but the aperiodic exponent was not associated with cognitive performance. After accounting for aperiodic activity, the NF1 group also had lower dominant oscillatory frequency than the control group. There was no significant interaction between NF1 diagnosis and age on PAF. There were no group differences in peak alpha power. ConclusionsWe demonstrate for the first time that the alterations to aperiodic activity in NF1 are consistent with the proposed mechanism of increased inhibitory tone. These findings show the potential of this paradigm for future pharmacological and brain stimulation trials investigating treatment-related changes in cortical function.

papers.title: A shared circuit architecture for multiscale signal recognition in crickets
papers.abstract: Communication signals often contain behaviorally relevant structure on multiple temporal scales. Short-timescale features are commonly thought to be recognized first and then integrated into longer-timescale representations. Whether a shared circuit can instead recognize multiple timescales remains unclear. Cricket calling songs provide a tractable test because millisecond-scale pulses are grouped into chirps lasting hundreds of milliseconds. We combined female phonotaxis with a mechanistic model of the identified pulse-recognition network to ask whether this circuitry can also generate chirp selectivity. In Gryllus bimaculatus, the model, originally parameterized from pulse-scale electrophysiology and behavior, recovered the main boundaries of chirp preference without fitting to chirp behavior. Coincidence detection generated the minimum chirp-duration requirement, whereas suppressive computations in the networks input neuron shaped the upper boundaries for chirp duty cycle and period. Across 14 species, varying these suppressive computations captured major differences in chirp tuning. These findings reveal a temporally interleaved serial circuit in which long-timescale selectivity begins upstream of completed short-timescale selectivity, offering an alternative to both conventional short-first hierarchies and parallel pathways.

papers.title: A piece-wise linear recurrent neural network identifies generalizable dynamics from neural activity during decision-making in rodents
papers.abstract: Alterations in impulsivity characterize several neuropsychiatric disorders, however the neural processes that underlie an impulsive choice have not been identified. A recent body of literature suggests that there may be generalizable aspects of neural representations across animals. Whether this is also true for dynamic rather than just static (like geometrical) properties of neural representations, and specifically in the context of impulsive behaviors, is less clear. Therefore, the goal of this study is to characterize generalizable features of latent dynamics that disambiguate an impulsive from non-impulsive choice across many different data sets and animals. A deep learning-based latent factor model was constructed from neural recordings that were acquired in rat anterior cingulate cortex while performing a delay discounting task, which is commonly used to assess impulsivity. Prior work shows this brain region is critical for the performance of this task. We leveraged piecewise linear recurrent neural networks (PLRNNs) to perform a nonlinear latent factor analysis across animals and experimental sessions. Our PLRNN explained a substantially larger percent of variance in fewer dimensions than linear approaches. We cross-validated performance of the model on test data and following the disruption of recurrent connectivity or auto-regressive latent dynamics. These tests confirmed that our fitting procedure consistently embedded generalizable neuronal dynamics within the PLRNN. Further, we found that the latent dynamics exhibited strong rotational features and progressed faster for impulsive choices. In summary, our model captures properties of the latent dynamics that are consistent across multiple data sets and disambiguate impulsive choices.

papers.title: Low-intensity ultrasound drives offline neuromodulation through passive membrane mechanisms in synaptically isolated hippocampal neurons
papers.abstract: Low-intensity ultrasound alters neuronal excitability long after exposure ends, but the basis of this offline effect is unclear and most proposed mechanisms require synaptic receptors. We recorded from cultured mouse hippocampal neurons in whole-cell current clamp, before and 20 min after 1 min of 850 kHz continuous-wave ultrasound at 0.5 W/cm2 or sham, with synaptic transmission blocked throughout, each neuron re-patched. Sonicated neurons remained intact and firing, yet depolarized, with smaller action potentials and more noise. A passive-membrane fit showed reduced capacitance and a depolarized leak reversal potential in every sonicated cell, with a shortened time constant and no detectable change in input conductance, while sham cells showed no significant change. Changes in the time constant and reversal potential, both independent of membrane area, indicate a modification of the membrane itself rather than a loss of area. Brief ultrasound therefore leaves a lasting, receptor-independent imprint on passive membrane properties.

papers.title: Hypothalamic tauP301L pathology disrupts pair bonding in monogamous prairie voles
papers.abstract: Although dementias primarily affect memory, they also disrupt our closest social relationships, resulting in elevated caregiver burden and worse patient outcomes. However, the mechanistic study of how pathology affects social attachments is limited by the use of laboratory rodents that do not form selective, long-term bonds. Here, in monogamous prairie voles, we expressed dementia-causing tauP301L in the paraventricular hypothalamus of 12- and 18-month-old animals, and separately, from birth through 18-months, across hippocampocortical regions. Hippocampocortical expression of tauP301L did not yield deficits in social or non-social dementia-related phenotypes. In contrast, tauP301L expressed in the hypothalamus yielded sex- and age-dependent social bonding deficits. 18-month males with hypothalamic tau pathology failed to form bonds and displayed blunted sociability, effects that converged across bonding assays. In addition, healthy 18-month males paired with a hypothalamic tau-expressing female also showed reduced partner preference, suggesting that pathology exerts vicarious effects on partners. Social behavior of both healthy females and those expressing tauP301L were unaffected. 18-month tauP301L males also showed elevated oxytocin fluorescence. These findings establish direct and vicarious disruptions to pair bonding induced by hypothalamic tau pathology in male prairie voles, potentially via altered oxytocin signaling.

papers.title: Single-cell spatial transcriptomics of inherited retinal degeneration reveals broad and focal organization of disease responses
papers.abstract: Inherited retinal degenerations are largely monogenic disorders characterized by progressive photoreceptor dysfunction and death. Although the transcriptomic responses to inherited degeneration are well-characterized, how these responses are spatially organized across the retinal axis has not been mapped. Here, we used seqFISH to spatially profile 173 cell identity and degeneration-associated genes with single-cell, single-transcript resolution in male wild-type and LCA5gt/gtmouse retinas at early, intermediate, and advanced disease stages. In early disease, rod injury and stress response markers were enriched in the superior retina, while rod function and identity markers were enriched in the inferior retina. Nested within the broader superior-inferior organization, a coordinated rod injury response comprising Edn2, Fgf2, Socs3, and Stat3 was organized into focal regions on the order of 100 m in width, with high-response regions directly adjacent to low-response regions. These focal regions were locally enriched for markers of Muller reactive gliosis and rod stress responses. Our single-cell spatiotemporal map reveals that transcriptional responses to degeneration vary at both the broad and focal scales, and offers a framework for investigating how local tissue properties and interactions among neighboring cells may contribute to disease progression.

papers.title: The olfactory ventricle: an overlooked and evolutionarily conserved feature of the mammalian brain
papers.abstract: The olfactory ventricle (OV), an anterior extension of the lateral ventricular system into the olfactory bulbs, is generally considered a transient developmental structure that closes during early postnatal life. However, this view largely derives from a limited number of laboratory models, and the evolutionary distribution and cellular organization of the adult OV remain poorly understood. Here, we combined a comparative survey of mammalian neuroanatomy with phylogenetic analyses and cellular characterization of the OV across species. We compiled anatomical data for 154 mammalian species spanning 26 orders and 80 families, revealing widespread persistence of a patent OV into adulthood. Phylogenetic analyses supported OV presence as the ancestral mammalian state and indicated that its absence is phylogenetically structured and consistent with repeated secondary losses. Chiroptera displayed multiple lineage-specific losses, whereas variation within Muridae extended to the intraspecific level, with contrasting OV persistence among Mus musculus and Rattus norvegicus populations. Comparative histological analyses in sheep, Peromyscus maniculatus, and CD1 mice revealed that, despite marked interspecific differences in OV morphology, the persistent ventricular region retains a conserved cellular organization characterized by progenitor- and glial-associated markers, proliferative cells, immature neuronal populations, and a differentiated apical/ciliary interface. Although these observations do not establish local neuronal production or demonstrate that the OV constitutes an autonomous neurogenic niche, their convergence across species indicates that the persistent adult OV is not simply an anatomically residual lumen but a specialized component of mammalian olfactory bulb organization. Together, our findings identify the OV as an ancestral and widely conserved feature of the mammalian brain and provide an evolutionary and cellular framework for investigating the developmental mechanisms controlling its persistence and its potential contribution to adult olfactory neurogenesis and plasticity.

papers.title: Shifts in neural representations, not gaze, track how people reinterpret ambiguous social scenes
papers.abstract: How do we come to "see" the same thing differently after hearing someone else's perspective? Revising an interpretation could reflect changes in how the brain represents the meaning of what we see, changes in how we visually sample the input, or both. To disentangle these mechanisms, we developed MindLibs, an adaptive fMRI and eye-tracking paradigm in which participants generate interpretations of ambiguous photographs and then view alternative interpretations chosen in real time to vary in semantic content from their own. Exposure to semantically distant alternatives revealed a strong link between reinterpretation as reported behaviorally and representational shifts in association cortex, but no systematic relationship between reinterpretation and changes in gaze. In particular, representational shifts in lateral default-mode network regions (DMN-B) predicted reinterpretation independently of shifts in frontoparietal, attention, and visual networks, and independently of whether gaze changed. In contrast, shifts in visual cortex tracked reinterpretation only when gaze also shifted, and contributed no unique variance beyond DMN-B. These findings identify higher-order conceptual reconfiguration, rather than perceptual resampling, as the primary account of how people revise the meaning of an ambiguous scene.

papers.title: Regional Similarity to Sex-Typical Young Adult Brain Architecture is a Longitudinal Correlate of Neuroinflammation and Depression in Later Adulthood
papers.abstract: Lifespan trajectories of psychiatric and neurodegenerative risk show robust overlap and marked sex differences. Nonetheless, their neurobiological underpinnings are still poorly understood. One potential culprit is the predominant categorical definition of sex, which overlooks the tapestry of sex-dependent and sex-independent features recently shown to typify each human brain. Shifting from a holistic, dichotomous approach to regionally specific, continuous assessments of sex differences in brain function could help identify individualized therapeutic targets for both psychiatric and neurological conditions. To probe the psychiatric and neurological relevance of functional alignment with sex-typical brain architecture, we analyzed longitudinal neuroimaging and clinical data from a healthy aging cohort (N = 353, aged 36-87 years). We identified complementary patterns of deviance from sex-typical brain architecture along the canonical sensorimotor-to-association axis, which overlapped areas enriched in microglial genes and genes regulating sex steroid metabolism. The two connectivity patterns differentiated longitudinally between psychiatric symptoms and neurodegeneration as a function sex and age: one connectivity pattern related to more severe future depression in younger women, whereas the second related to later neurodegeneration (higher GFAP and pT217 blood concentration) and poorer fluid cognition (inhibition, episodic memory, processing speed, working memory) in older men. The aforementioned effects showed some context-specificity, as they involved connectivity patterns characterized during awake rest and cognitive control, but not associative memory performance. Taken together, our findings attest to the value of integrating regionally specific, continuous assessments of sex differences in brain function with inflammation-relevant biomarkers in order to support precision medicine approaches across the life course.

papers.title: Bio-inspired chromatophore network model generates dynamic skin patterns akin to those observed in cephalopods
papers.abstract: Cephalopod skin exhibits a wide range of dynamic visual displays, including traveling waves, light/dark flashes, and flickering, all generated by muscle-regulated expansion and retraction of pigment-filled elastic sacs known as chromatophores. While central neural control is essential for high-level body-wide pattern coordination, experimental evidence from excised and denervated skin reveals that intricate spatiotemporal patterns can also emerge spontaneously in the skin. This raises questions about the respective roles of central versus peripheral control. To determine the simplest control necessary to generate such patterns, we developed ChromatoNet, a biophysical model of chromatophore arrays that includes mechanical interactions on 1- and 2-dimensional lattices with the excitability properties of radial muscles. With minimal external input, our modified Morris--Lecar model reproduces a rich repertoire of skin dynamics, including spontaneous flickering as well as traveling and spiral waves. Both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked waves emerge at an intrinsic resonant frequency, determined by model parameters. Propagation speeds remain stable across conditions and are consistent with the range observed in denervated skin preparations. The model generates diverse output states in response to local couplings and the time-dependence and shape of the input stimulation, with little top-down direction. The results provide a proof-of-principle that chromatophore/muscle dynamics with minimal central neural driving can produce rich dynamic patterns.

papers.title: A psychophysical characterization of tactile and temperature perception on the human torso
papers.abstract: Numerous studies have been conducted to investigate touch on the hand and forearm, but less is known about the rest of the body, particularly the torso and breasts, which play an important role in affective touch. We conducted psychophysical tests on three skin sites on the torso: upper breast, nipple-areola complex (NAC), and under the breast, as well as on two control sites: palm and forearm. We studied touch pleasantness and intensity by applying gentle caress-like strokes using a soft brush, and measured temperature and tactile detection thresholds. The results show an inverted U-shaped relationship for pleasantness over increasing stroking velocity for all skin sites, although we found some differences between sites, particularly at 30 cm.s-1, where participants found stroking on the NAC to be more intense and women additionally found it to be less pleasant. For temperature detection, we found that the NAC was more sensitive in men. For tactile detection, we mainly observed that the areola was far less sensitive than the other areas. Together, these results provide insights into tactile perception in the torso on a fundamental level, which can be applied to understanding how to regain sensations after mastectomy.

papers.title: Electrical stimulation of the human pulvinar generates visual percepts
papers.abstract: Visual prostheses have targeted early structures in the visual pathway, including the retina, optic nerve, lateral geniculate nucleus, and visual cortex, to generate visual percepts. Stimulation of higher-order visual regions, which may better encode complex visual features, remains relatively unexplored. We tested whether electrical stimulation of the medial and inferior pulvinar elicits visual percepts in a patient with medically refractory epilepsy undergoing invasive seizure monitoring with intracranial electroencephalography. Bipolar stimulation (30 biphasic pulses, 0.5 ms per phase, 3 mA, 1 Hz) was delivered between adjacent pulvinar contacts while eye movements were tracked. Stimulation of different electrode pairs elicited visual percepts at distinct retinotopic locations (p = 0.010). Stimulation also altered cortical activity, producing an early power increase followed by gamma desynchronization in occipital and parietal regions (p < 0.001) and beta desynchronization in the lateral temporal region (p < 0.01). These findings suggest that pulvinar stimulation can generate visual percepts and modulate distributed cortical networks, supporting further investigation of the pulvinar as a target for vision restoration.

papers.title: Wavelet Transform Coherence Under Controlled Temporal Correspondence and Social Co-Presence: Implications for fNIRS Hyperscanning
papers.abstract: Interpersonal neural synchrony research using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) frequently relies on wavelet transform coherence (WTC) to quantify temporal correspondence between cortical signals. Yet, whether WTC reliably recovers experimentally defined differences in signal correspondence remains insufficiently established. Here, we evaluated WTC using an auditory-guided finger-tapping paradigm in which matching and non-matching temporal structures were compared within participants and between dyad members during individual and joint performance. Task-evoked analyses confirmed reliable recruitment of contralateral motor and premotor regions across both contexts, whereas the ipsilateral motor cortex was significantly recruited only during joint performance and was the only region differing between sessions. WTC sensitivity was strongly modulated by social co-presence. Within participants, WTC failed to discriminate matching from non-matching temporal structures during individual performance, whereas robust matching-related increases emerged during joint performance, particularly in contralateral motor and premotor regions. Between participants, WTC showed limited and region-specific discrimination when participants were tested separately, but higher coherence for matching temporal structures emerged during joint performance, particularly in motor regions. These findings show that WTC can recover experimentally defined temporal correspondence between fNIRS signals, but that this sensitivity is not context-independent. The within-participant results further suggest that social co-presence may alter the temporal dynamics of the individual neural signals themselves. WTC should therefore be interpreted as a context-sensitive measure whose meaning depends on the functional and social processes generating the signals being compared.

papers.title: Bone Marrow-Derived Cells Fuse with Bergmann Glia in Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis
papers.abstract: Bone marrow-derived cells (BMDCs) can infiltrate the brain and adopt new identities through transdifferentiation or fusion, yet their interactions with specific neural cells remain poorly defined. We examined BMDC fusion with Bergmann glia (BG), a key cerebellar support cell, in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. After bone marrow transplantation, BMDCs fused with BG to form heterokaryons, retaining BG morphology and molecular markers. These heterokaryons contained donor and host nuclei that differed in both morphology and transcriptional activity. Remarkably, the BMDC nucleus localized not only to the soma but also along BG processes. This discovery identifies BMDC-BG fusion as a previously unrecognized form of glial plasticity, opening avenues for therapeutic strategies aimed at potentiating glial-mediated repair.

papers.title: A comprehensive physiological dataset of pain and aversive modalities for pain biomarkers research
papers.abstract: While progress has been made in identifying pain biomarkers using neuroimaging, the development of reliable EEG-based biomarkers remains challenging, limited by small sample sizes and the lack of adequate control conditions. We present a comprehensive dataset from 125 pain-free adults, comprising electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings, and behavioural, sociodemographic, and psychological data. Galvanic skin response and electrocardiogram data were also recorded in a subset of participants (n = 76). Participants received two sustained painful stimulations (thermal, chemical) and two sustained aversive non-painful stimulations (auditory, taste), each delivered twice (with and without continuous intensity ratings). Data are provided in Brain Imaging Data Structure format, where all physiological, stimulus-related, and behavioural data are synchronized within the EEG data files for easy access and analysis. Technical validation confirmed data integrity, with spectral and physiological analyses showing responses associated with stimulus intensity and subjective pain/unpleasantness levels. By providing multimodal physiological data across painful and non-painful aversive conditions, this initiative represents a valuable resource for developing or validating biomarkers and exploring the multidimensional nature of pain perception.

papers.title: Resolution-aware spectral parameterization reveals robust context-dependent aperiodic EEG dynamics during real-world table tennis
papers.abstract: Mobile EEG can link neuroimaging to natural behavior, but effects recorded during movement, and sport in particular, are difficult to interpret because neural activity overlaps with signals from movement, muscle activity, and cable movement artifacts. We analyzed the OpenNeuro Real World Table Tennis dataset to test whether peri-hit spectral activity could be analyzed and how it differed between human-opponent and ball-machine play. Data from 25 participants comprising EEG, noise-layers, EMG and motion recordings was analyzed with pre-hit, impact, and post-hit windows. EEG power bands were residualized using trial-level root mean square from noise-layer, EMG, and motion/miscellaneous channels. Spectral parameterization modeled spectra as an aperiodic component plus periodic peaks. The principal short-window model was resolution-aware; sensitivity analyses reduced model complexity, used a 2.0-s peri-hit subwindow (-1.0 to +1.0 s), or disabled periodic fitting. Results showed residualized alpha and beta power was lower during ball-machine play, including pre-hit posterior alpha power. The clearest context difference was a higher ball-machine aperiodic exponent over posterior and parietal sensors, corresponding to a steeper broadband spectral slope. Posterior post-hit means were 0.451 and 0.606 for human-opponent and ball-machine play, respectively. A focal parietal effect persisted across specifications. The results support artifact-informed, resolution-aware spectral analysis as an effective approach for detecting robust spectral differences between naturalistic visuomotor contexts and suggest that EEG may provide useful information about the processes engaged by different practice environments, without establishing a single cognitive or physiological mechanism or demonstrating a training outcome.

papers.title: Facial color properties affect perceived age.
papers.abstract: Age is a fundamental social attribute that affects rights, responsibilities and even social status. Color information of the face can affect perceived age, but the nature of its contribution, independent of luminance information, remains underexplored. To better characterize the role of color in age perception, we conducted two experiments. In our first experiment, we tested whether natural age-related changes in facial color alone can drive changes in perceived age. In our second experiment, we manipulated red-green contrast across faces aged 18-91 and tested the effect of this manipulation of perceived youthfulness. Our findings demonstrate that natural age-related color changes do provide cues for age perception, dissociable from luminance information. We also found that the optimal red-green contrast level to make faces look the youngest was significantly higher than the originals, meaning that faces tended to appear younger when their redness was accentuated, even though average face redness increases with age. Our analysis revealed that younger faces required greater increases in redness level compared to their older counterparts to achieve the youngest appearance. These results suggest that the spatial distribution of redness contributes to apparent youthfulness, especially in younger faces.

papers.title: On-demand surround suppression explains the spatiotemporal window of the tilt illusion
papers.abstract: What we see at one location depends on what surrounds it. Such contextual e[ff]ects are thought to arise from neural signals that travel across the retinotopic representations.Because these signals need more time to travel longer distances, a more distant surround should influence perception most strongly when presented earlier, compensating for its delay. We tested this prediction in human observers using a visual illusion in which a central target appears tilted away from the orientation of its surround (tilt illusion). Measuring the temporal window of this illusion using psychophysical reverse correlation revealed the opposite: the most e[ff]ective surround occurred progressively later as distance increased. Computational modelling demonstrated that this reversal is explained if the visual system sends out a query that recruits contextual information on demand. Perceptual appearance may thus be constructed through temporally unfolding interactions in which context is actively gathered, not passively received.

papers.title: Netrin signaling shapes sexually dimorphic neurite branching of a sex-shared interneuron in C. elegans
papers.abstract: Sexually dimorphic behaviors arise from underlying differences in neural circuit architecture between the sexes, yet the molecular mechanisms that establish these structural differences remain poorly understood. In Caenorhabditis elegans, the sex-shared interneuron AVG exhibits sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity, offering a model for investigating the development of sexually dimorphic neuronal morphology. Here, we identified that AVG displays male-specific neurite branching and demonstrated that the conserved axon guidance cue UNC-6/Netrin and its receptor UNC-40/DCC are essential for this structural remodeling. Cell-specific manipulation of sexual identity revealed that male identity confers branching competence to AVG. Loss of UNC-6 or UNC-40 abolished branch formation, whereas loss of the alternate Netrin receptor UNC-5/Unc5 had no detectable effect. Cell-specific rescue experiments showed that UNC-40 functions in AVG through its UNC-6 binding domains. Furthermore, genetic ablation of the male-specific presynaptic neuron PCA, which expresses unc-6, diminished AVG branch length, establishing PCA as a candidate local source of UNC-6. Together, our findings support a model in which presynaptic UNC-6/Netrin cues from male-specific neurons promote dimorphic neurite branching in sex-shared neurons, illustrating how evolutionarily conserved signaling molecules are redeployed during sexual maturation to sculpt sex-specific neural circuits.
